contentHtml:
"His friends have all had a growth spurt and he hasn't." Height comes up in almost every consultation I have with parents of teenage athletes in India, more than almost any other single topic. It sits right at the intersection of two big anxieties — sporting selection and general wellbeing, which is exactly why it gets targeted with a lot of confident-sounding, unproven advice.

This post is the honest version: what genuinely influences a teenager's growth, what doesn't, and where nutrition actually fits in. It follows directly from our RED-S guide, which already flags energy deficiency as a threat to growth trajectory, and our iron deficiency blog, since iron status also plays into this.

How Much of Height Is Actually Genetic?

More than most parents expect. Large twin studies show the genetic contribution to height rises steadily through childhood and reaches roughly 70–90% by adolescence; comparative twin data across countries puts adult height heritability at around 80–90% in men and somewhat lower, more variable levels in women.

But genetics only sets the ceiling.

Whether a teenager actually reaches it depends on what's happening at the growth plates (also called epiphyseal plates), the soft cartilage zones near the ends of the long bones where new bone is laid down during childhood and puberty.

This is the only place in the body where height is actually being built. Growth plates are active for a limited window: they gradually harden and "close" once puberty ends. It's typically earlier in girls (around 14–16) than boys (around 16–18). Moreover, once a growth plate has fused, no amount of nutrition, sleep, or training can reopen it or add further height.

This is what makes the growing years a genuinely time-limited opportunity, not an ongoing one. During that open window, growth plates need a steady supply of energy, protein, calcium, and vitamin D to build bone at the rate genetics has programmed. An energy or nutrient gap during this specific period, not before it, not after it. This causes a teenager to fall short of their own genetic height potential.

That's a meaningful and worthwhile thing to get right, but it's a different promise than "add inches," and I'd rather be upfront about that than sell something nutrition can't deliver.

Why the Growing Years Matter So Much for an Athlete

If you are wondering how to grow taller, roughly 90% of adult bone mass and the majority of adult height are built by the end of adolescence, which makes the teenage training years a genuinely sensitive window, not because training is risky, but because getting energy and nutrients wrong during a growth spurt has more consequences than it would a few years later.

The biggest, most under-recognised risk isn't a missing nutrient; it's not eating enough overall for a training load layered on top of a growth spurt. This is precisely the energy availability problem we've written about in detail in our RED-S guide: when a teenage athlete's calorie intake doesn't cover both training demands and growth demands, the body deprioritises growth to protect more immediately essential functions.

Sleep: The Most Underrated Piece of the Growth Puzzle

Parents ask me about protein and supplements far more than they ask about sleep, and that's backwards. The majority of daily growth hormone secretion happens during sleep, concentrated in deep sleep, and adolescence is the peak period for growth hormone output. This is when the pubertal growth spurt is largely driven.

This is a real, practical gap in Indian teenage athlete households. Late-night homework, early-morning practice, coaching commutes, and exam pressure routinely push a training teenager well under the recommended 8–10 hours a night.

One review of high school athletes found that over 79% were sleeping fewer than 8 hours a night, well below the recommended range for adolescents.

If sleep is being cut short, that's arguably a bigger lever for growth than any single food or supplement — and it's free.

How to Grow Taller: Nutrients That Genuinely Support Linear Growth

Within the boundaries genetics sets, a handful of nutrients have real evidence behind their role in linear growth:

NutrientWhy it mattersGood sources
ProteinBuilding block for tissue growth, needed at adequate (not excess) levelsEggs, dal, curd, paneer, milk, chicken/fish
CalciumDeposited into bone at peak rate during the growth spurtMilk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame (til)
ZincShown to have a measurable positive effect on linear growth in nutrition intervention studiesPumpkin seeds, chickpeas, whole grains, eggs, dairy
Vitamin DWorks with calcium for bone mineralisation; deficiency is linked to poorer height growthSunlight exposure, eggs, fortified milk
IronAlso tied to linear growth, not just energyDark leafy greens, jaggery, legumes, eggs, meat

Worth being honest about: more protein is not automatically better for growth. One large cross-sectional study in adolescents actually found very high protein intake associated with shorter stature. Each incremental increase in already-elevated protein intake was linked to reduced height and height-for-age.

This finding is almost certainly explained by families overfeeding protein to children who are already shorter than expected, rather than protein itself causing shorter height, but it's a useful reminder: adequate protein supports growth, loading up on protein powder or extra portions doesn't accelerate it further, and total energy and micronutrient adequacy matter more than protein alone.

The Myth I Hear Most: "Weight Training Will Stunt His Growth"

This is, by far, the most common growth-related myth I correct — and it stops a lot of teenage athletes from strength training that would actually help their sport. Current pediatric and sports-medicine guidance is clear that properly supervised resistance training is safe for adolescents and does not interfere with growth. Multiple reviews have found resistance training results in increased IGF-1 (a growth-related hormone) with no detrimental effect on linear growth.

The fear traces back to growth plate injuries, but growth plate injuries are actually far more common in unsupervised contact sports like football and basketball than in supervised strength training programs. The real risk factor is poor technique and excessive, unsupervised loading — not resistance training itself. If anything, weight-bearing resistance training supports bone density during exactly the years bone mass is being built.

What About "Height-Increasing" Supplements?

Almost every parent has come across a powder, tablet, or drink marketed to "increase height" for teenagers. I'd steer clear of this category. No credible evidence shows any commercial supplement adds height beyond what an adequate, balanced diet already provides, and given how strongly genetics and overall nutrition (not a single additive) drive growth, these products sell a promise nutrition science can't back.

If there's a genuine gap, say, confirmed low vitamin D or iron on a blood test, that's a targeted, evidence-based fix, not a generic "height supplement." This is the same food-first-then-targeted-testing approach we use at Pragmatic Nutrition.

Practical Checklist for Supporting a Growing Teen Athlete

  • Make sure total calorie intake actually covers training load plus growth. This is the single biggest lever, more than any individual nutrient
  • Protect 8–10 hours of sleep, since this is when the bulk of growth hormone is released
  • Include a daily calcium source (milk, curd, paneer, ragi) alongside adequate protein — not excess protein
  • Don't fear supervised strength training; it doesn't stunt growth, and it supports bone health
  • If growth genuinely seems to be lagging (not just "shorter than a teammate"), get it properly assessed rather than reaching for a supplement — a sports nutritionist can check growth trajectory against family height patterns and rule out an energy or nutrient gap

My Stand

Height is one of the areas where I see the most anxiety-driven spending and the least evidence-based guidance, especially in Indian sporting households where a child's height can feel tied to their entire sporting future.

The honest picture is that genetics sets the ceiling, and nutrition's real job is making sure a growing, training teenager doesn't fall short of their own potential through under-eating, poor sleep, or an untreated deficiency — not adding inches beyond what their biology allows.

That's a less exciting story than a height-boosting supplement, but it's the one backed by evidence, and it's the one I'll always give a parent honestly.

If you're concerned about your young athlete's growth alongside their training load, it's worth a proper assessment rather than guessing.

FAQs

Can nutrition actually increase a teenager's height?

Nutrition can't override genetics, which accounts for roughly 70–90% of adult height. What good nutrition does is prevent a teenager from falling short of their own genetic height potential due to under-eating, poor sleep, or a nutrient deficiency.


Does weight training stunt growth in teenage athletes?

No. Current research and pediatric guidelines consistently find no evidence that properly supervised resistance training damages growth plates or reduces adult height — growth plate injuries are actually more common in unsupervised contact sports.

Does more protein help a teenager grow taller?

Not beyond adequate intake. Excess protein hasn't been shown to accelerate growth, and total energy, sleep, and micronutrient status matter more than simply increasing protein further.

How much sleep does a teenage athlete need for growth?

8–10 hours a night is recommended for adolescents, since the majority of daily growth hormone secretion happens during deep sleep — a commonly under-met target for training teenagers with heavy school and practice schedules.

Are height-increasing supplements for teenagers effective?

There's no credible evidence that commercial "height-increasing" supplements add height beyond what an adequate, balanced diet already supports. A targeted fix for a confirmed deficiency (like low vitamin D or iron) is a different, evidence-based matter.

When should a parent get a teenage athlete's growth checked by a doctor?

If growth appears to be genuinely lagging relative to family height patterns and expected growth trajectory, not just "shorter than a teammate"- rather than assuming it will self-correct or reaching for a supplement.
